**Concert Pitch**

On the phone she said the piano hadn't been tuned since her husband died, then corrected herself: since before he died. He'd stopped playing first. That was eleven years ago. I said Thursday would work, and after she hung up I sat a minute with the length of it. Eleven years is a short thing to say and a long thing to be.

Her house sat back from the road behind two pines, curtains drawn against the afternoon, a stone rabbit by the steps with its ears worn soft. Mrs. Voss was small in the doorway, smaller in the hall. The front room held a lamp, a chair, and the piano — a Baldwin upright, walnut gone dull, a coaster under one leg to save the floor. The keys had yellowed like teeth, like old book pages. On the music rack sat one piece of sheet music, curled at the corners: "Summertime," arranged for easy piano. On the lid, a photograph of a man in shirtsleeves at the bench, caught mid-laugh, looking back at the camera as if the person holding it had just said something.

I raised the lid. Dust inside like felt, like snow that had been falling indoors for years. I took out my hammer and mutes and fork, struck my A against the piano's A, and the piano answered from somewhere down around 1950 — flat, low, a sound with a coat of dust on it.

"You want the window open?" Mrs. Voss said from her chair. "It gets close in here."

"I'm fine," I said. Not quite true. I'd just rather hear the piano than the road.

Here is the whole craft, if you want it. When two notes are nearly the same note, they fight. You hear a wobble — a slow throb, a pulse heard through a wall. You catch the pin with the hammer and ease the string tighter, and the beats slow. Slower, slower. When they stop — when there's nothing left but one clean tone — the note is in tune. Tuning is sitting with a pulse until it settles. Everything else is grip.

Mrs. Voss watched my hands.

"Walter played every night," she said. "After dinner. Same song." She tipped her head at the music rack. "He got the middle wrong every time. I'd say, Walter, you're playing it wrong again, and he'd say, I know where it goes. I just like it better here."

While I worked the treble she asked if I wanted more coffee, and I said no, and my own question got out ahead of me: why now, after eleven years?

She thought about it honestly, letting me watch her think. "You get out of the habit of asking for things," she said. "A piano tuner. A doctor. A ride to the store. Every year you don't ask, it costs more to start again." She looked at the piano. "This morning it cost less."

Down in the bass I found the truth of it. The piano wasn't a little flat; it had settled — the whole instrument half a step under the world and sagging beneath that. A soundboard is a thin plank of spruce holding back thousands of pounds of string pull, and it had spent eleven years letting go. Two pins in the treble spun loose in their holes like bad teeth. To haul it up to concert pitch now — to A440, the pitch the whole world agreed on, mostly by accident — I'd have to put all that tension back at once, into strings that had lived low so long they'd gone brittle. I could break one. I could break several. I could do everything right and crack the plate, and then the piano is furniture.

I gave her the plain version. "I can't bring it back to concert pitch," I said. "Not today. Probably not ever, without breaking things that can't be fixed. What I can do is tune it to itself. Put the fork away, take the piano's own A for the top of the ladder, and build every note back into agreement with every other. It'll sit a little lower than the world. It'll sound like itself."

Mrs. Voss looked at the piano for a while. The lamp buzzed.

"Everything else in this house is," she said.

So that's what I did.

The middle hours are the part nobody sees. Wedge in, hammer on, strike, listen, pull, listen. Note by note, interval by interval, teaching the piano to agree with itself again, the beats slowing all afternoon like a heart coming down. The light moved across the floor and up the far wall. Somewhere in the third hour Mrs. Voss fell asleep in the chair, coffee cooling on the arm, and I worked quieter, which was pointless; she'd spent forty years falling asleep to worse.

When I finished, I tested it the way you're supposed to, banging chords and octaves hard enough to wake the dead, or at least his widow. Nothing moved. The piano held. It agreed with itself top to bottom, low and warm and half a step shy of the world — a radio from another country playing a song you almost know.

I packed up, and the latches woke her. She came to the door with a checkbook and wrote the check with a hand that had decided not to shake.

"How long will it hold?" she asked.

"Years. Long as nobody slams it. Long as the room stays even."

"Good," she said.

At the door, case in hand, she said, "Play something."

"I don't play," I said. "I tune them." It was true. In thirty years I've had my hands inside a thousand pianos and never learned to play one.

She looked at me a moment, then went past me into the room and sat down at the bench. Her hands hovered over the keys like she was checking whether they still worked. Then they moved, and I knew the song before I knew her playing — "Summertime," slow, halting, full of mistakes. And when she reached the middle she got it wrong. Wrong the same way. The note bent to where Walter had always put it, because that's where she'd learned it, wrong, across forty years of dinners.

I stood in the doorway with my coat on and did what I do. Listened for the beats — the wobble, the fight, the pulse that means something's off, something's low, something's not agreed.

There weren't any.

The user has given me complete creative freedom: 1000 words, write whatever comes to me. This is one of the most open-ended prompts possible, and also one of the most interesting. There's no constraint on topic, genre, form, or tone. The only constraint is length (approximately 1000 words).

What should I write? Let me think about what would be genuinely good here, not just filler.

Options:
1. A short story — fiction is the classic choice for "write whatever comes to you"
2. An essay — reflective, personal, about something
3. A meditation on the prompt itself (too meta, probably clichéd)
4. Poetry — but 1000 words of poetry is a lot; could do a long-form poem or prose poem
5. A hybrid piece — something that plays with form
6. Creative nonfiction — a memory, real or invented

The prompt "write whatever comes to you" invites spontaneity, but good spontaneous writing still needs craft. I think the best response is a piece of writing that:

- Goes somewhere — has movement, an arc, even a small one
- Feels alive, not generated
- Isn't just competent filler

- A translator who finds something odd in a text
